children: Since the 1970s, the Federal Reserve has held the stance of “looking through” supply shocks and only responding if the resulting inflation bleeds into other industries or if inflation expectations become unanchored. But the more frequent supply shocks seen recently may require a new approach, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday.

"We seem to have entered a period where large supply shocks — from wars, tariffs, weather, supply chain disruptions, oil shocks, and so on — have become a regular feature of the economy," Goolsbee said in a speech at the Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum Event in London, England. "My argument is that in this new environment, there are some supply shocks that central banks should not simply look through — namely, the persistent ones."

It has been standard to hold off on monetary policy adjustment when a supply shock boosts in inflation because the shock often resolves relatively quickly on its own or may be a one-time price adjustment that's doesn't feed an inflationary trend. But that may no longer be the case.
He explained, "A cost shock that lasts multiple years forces us to revisit the rationale for looking through. No one said to automatically look through persistent inflationary supply shocks."

Inflation in the U.S. has exceeded the Fed's 2% goal for more than five years. Goolsbee pointed to the supply shock caused by COVID-19, followed by tariffs and the war in the Gulf. The resulting inflation demands that the Fed act, he said.

"If the forecast calls for large, persistent, recurring shocks, the central bank still has to restore price stability under its legal mandate — and the only way to bring inflation down is to raise rates and narrow the gap between supply and demand, even if it’s not in the exact same sectors where the cost shocks are occurring," Goolsbee said.

In the current economic landscape, the Chicago Fed president is keeping a close eye on elevated inflation in the service sector and on any evidence that AI data center construction is raising output beyond what the economy can absorb. "Either could be signs of old-fashioned demand overheating — and if demand overheats, there is no ambiguity about how the Fed needs to respond. Both are areas of concern in the recent data," he said.
On the supply side, forecasters have been pushing further out the date for when inflation will peak and then fall.
"We need evidence that these shocks are actually fading, or it’s hard to see a credible path back to 2% inflation — and harder still to justify continuing to look through them," Goolsbee said.
The Fed's policy response to persistent supply shocks may not need to be as large as its response to overheated demand, "but it won't be painless either," he noted.

"This is exactly the painful trade-off between employment and inflation that stagflationary shocks always impose on a central bank," Goolsbee concluded in his prepared remarks. "Unfortunately, in environments like that, the only way back is the hard way."

title: The Fed shouldn't 'look through' some supply shocks, Chicago Fed's Goolsbee says
